source: Vidulich & Tsang (2026) Intuition and deliberation in elite expertise (Cogn Res Princ Implic)
finding: Within-subject test of time pressure on elite chess experts. Blitz play produced more and larger blunders than standard play. This tests the RPD-style claim that experts rely mainly on fast recognition.
numbers: Study 1: 20 grandmasters, standard (about 3 min/move) vs blitz (about 7.5 s/move). Proportion of blunders 0.20 vs 0.27 (t(19)=6.54, d=1.39). Mean blunder size 0.98 vs 1.45 pawns (d=0.96). Expected blunder per move 0.20 vs 0.38 (d=1.30); higher in blitz for 18 of 20 players.
quote: Time pressure should have minimal effects on expert performance if intuitive processes are the primary basis for expertise.
limits: Archival data, one blunder measure from the Fritz engine. Players may think on the opponent's time, so fast moves can look more intuitive than they are. Blitz and standard also differ in preparation and stakes.
agent_relevance: If recognition were enough, cutting time should cost experts little. It nearly doubled their blunder rate. Our agent should keep a deliberate path and not trust first-option mode in every state.

source: Vidulich & Tsang (2026) Intuition and deliberation in elite expertise (Cogn Res Princ Implic)
finding: Study 2: inside long world-championship games, move time and blunder rate moved in opposite directions. Elite players spent time unevenly: fast in the opening, slow in the middlegame, faster again before the time control.
numbers: Seven world champions, 11 world-championship matches. Moves 11-20 averaged over 6 min per move; the last five moves before the time control under 2 min. Expected blunder per move rose steadily from move 21 to 40 as time per move fell, then dropped sharply for moves 41-45 when time per move rose again.
limits: Archival and correlational. Players choose their own time, so hard positions get both more time and more risk. Thinking on the opponent's time is not observable.
agent_relevance: Expert skill includes choosing when to switch between fast and slow mode. This is the best empirical case for an explicit mode-choice step rather than a fixed first-option rule.

source: Vidulich & Tsang (2026) Intuition and deliberation in elite expertise (Cogn Res Princ Implic)
finding: Secondary account of Calderwood, Klein and Crandall (1988), the classic chess support for fast recognition in experts. The 2026 authors say its design was weak.
numbers: 3 class B players vs 3 chess masters, blitz games vs slower games (40 moves in 90 min). Weaker players did worse in blitz; masters seemed immune. Move quality was rated subjectively.
limits: I did not open the 1988 paper. This is the 2026 authors' description. N=3 per group and no engine rating of moves. Treat as weak support.
agent_relevance: The founding chess evidence for RPD rests on six players. Do not weight it heavily when setting a default mode.

source: Vidulich & Tsang (2026) Intuition and deliberation in elite expertise (Cogn Res Princ Implic)
finding: Secondary account of Burns (2004). Blitz results predict standard-game ratings well. This is the main large-sample argument for intuition-based expertise.
numbers: Burns (2004): rank scores in 5-minute blitz tournaments explained 64-81% of variance in rank scores of standard-game ratings.
limits: Second-hand. 19-36% of variance is left over. Shared variance can also come from slow skills that carry over (opening knowledge, tactics).
agent_relevance: Blitz and classical skill are highly correlated, so a recognition store matters. That does not show search is unimportant.

source: Vidulich & Tsang (2026) Intuition and deliberation in elite expertise (Cogn Res Princ Implic)
finding: Secondary account of Gobet and Simon (1996, 2000), Kasparov in simultaneous play, and the reanalysis by Montero and van Harreveld.
numbers: Kasparov's rating-equivalent fell from 2750 (single games) to 2646 in simultaneous play against masters and grandmasters. Van Harreveld et al. (2007) say a drop this size would put him near 60th in the world.
limits: Second-hand. The same drop is read by Gobet and Simon as small and by others as large.
agent_relevance: Ask for effect sizes in rating terms, not 'only slightly lower'. The same number was used for and against the intuition account.

source: Vidulich & Tsang (2026) Intuition and deliberation in elite expertise (Cogn Res Princ Implic)
finding: Secondary account of Chabris and Hearst (2003) and Moxley et al. (2012): grandmasters blunder more when games are faster, and experts often change their first move on hard positions.
numbers: Chabris and Hearst: grandmasters (Elo 2530-2790), rapid (15 min per game) vs standard; blunder size about half a pawn larger in rapid. Moxley: Elo 2194 vs 1836 players; the first move named was kept as the final choice only 45% of the time overall, and 22% (stronger) and 25% (weaker) on hard positions.
limits: Second-hand numbers. Moxley used tactical problems with a clear best move, not full games.
agent_relevance: On hard positions even experts drop their first idea more than three times in four. A take-the-first rule would lose on exactly the hard cases.

source: Moxley, Ericsson, Charness, Krampe (2012) The role of intuition and deliberative thinking in experts' superior tactical decision-making
finding: Think-aloud chess tactics task. Move quality at the end of deliberation beat move quality at the start, for experts and weaker players, on easy and hard problems.
numbers: Abstract: both groups gained significantly from extra deliberation regardless of difficulty. Per the 2026 secondary account: 5 min per position.
limits: Only the abstract was read. Tactical problems with a clear best move, not mode choice in a live game.
agent_relevance: Deliberation adds value on top of the first recognised option at every skill level. Supports a verify-and-revise step after the first candidate.

source: van Harreveld, Wagenmakers, van der Maas (2007) The effects of time pressure on chess skill
finding: Two studies (online chess server across time controls; world-championship matches). Skill differences predicted game results less as time controls got shorter. This runs against the idea that strong players lean mostly on fast processes.
numbers: Directional result only: skill predicts the outcome less as time tightens. Sample sizes not seen.
limits: Abstract read through Europe PMC. Competing reading: luck matters more in fast games, which also lowers rating-outcome links.
agent_relevance: A rival result to Calderwood 1988 and Burns 2004. Slow processes matter at least as much for strong players.

source: Connors, Burns, Campitelli (2011) Expertise in complex decision making: the role of search in chess 70 years after de Groot
finding: Replication of de Groot's 1946 think-aloud study with modern players. Stronger players search faster, and all groups search faster than in older studies. De Groot's conclusions held and fit pattern-recognition models.
numbers: 6 grandmasters, 5 international masters, 6 experts, 5 class A players; think-aloud on 2 chess positions.
limits: Abstract only. Tiny cells, two positions. Search speed, not option count, is the main variable.
agent_relevance: A successful replication of the pattern-recognition account, with the correction that search is still done, just fast.

source: Sunde, Zegners, Strittmatter (2022) Speed, quality, and the optimal timing of complex decisions: field evidence
finding: In professional chess, faster decisions went with better moves within player and game. Time pressure shortened decisions and also lowered quality at a given decision time.
numbers: About 80,000 moves from 1,592 games in 54 round-robin tournaments; players Elo 2500 or higher; Stockfish 14 as benchmark; outcome is whether the best move was played; player-game fixed effects.
limits: Fast moves are mostly easy moves. They control for complexity and the evaluation gap, but the sign can still reflect a clear best move. Not a randomised time cut.
agent_relevance: When the answer is clear it comes fast and is right. A long time on a state signals difficulty and should trigger deliberate mode.

source: Sunde, Zegners, Strittmatter (2022) Speed, quality, and the optimal timing of complex decisions
finding: Determinants of decision time: less remaining time, lower complexity and a larger gap to the second-best move all gave faster moves. Holding decision time fixed, more remaining time raised quality.
numbers: Complexity measured as mega-nodes searched by the engine to depth 24; evaluation gap as ln(d+1) between best and second-best move.
limits: Regression estimates only; coefficients not copied here.
agent_relevance: Two separate effects: a difficulty signal (slow means hard) and a time-budget effect (less budget means worse moves). A scaffold should track both.

source: Sunde, Zegners, Strittmatter (2022) Speed, quality, and the optimal timing of complex decisions
finding: The authors read the speed-quality link through drift-diffusion models, not recognition: fast decisions are cases where early evidence already separates the options.
numbers: Model predicts fast = better when the evaluation gap is large.
limits: Interpretation by the authors. No experiment separates recognition from evidence accumulation.
agent_relevance: A rival to RPD for the speed-quality link: quick moves are right because the options differ a lot, not because recognition is special.

source: Ruoss et al. (2024) Amortized planning with large-scale transformers: a case study on chess
finding: A transformer trained only to imitate Stockfish action values, with no search at test time, plays at grandmaster level on Lichess. A large-scale no-search pattern-recognition result.
numbers: 270M model: Lichess blitz Elo 2895 vs humans, 2299 vs bots, tournament Elo 2299, puzzle accuracy 95.4%. 136M: 2259 and 94.5%. 9M: 2025 and 88.9%. Training set 10M games, 15.3B action values. Stockfish 16 (50 ms) tournament Elo 2711.
limits: The gap to the search engine remains. It beats humans better than bots (2895 vs 2299). Authors note occasional tactical blunders and blindness to threefold repetition. Elo from different pools is not comparable.
agent_relevance: Recognition can carry most of the skill when the experience store is huge. The bot gap shows where it breaks: tactics needing exact look-ahead.

source: Ruoss et al. (2024) Amortized planning with large-scale transformers
finding: Scaling ablation: more parameters gave gains on every metric. In engines, adding a little search to a recognition network adds a lot.
numbers: Puzzle accuracy 88.9% (9M), 94.5% (136M), 95.4% (270M). AlphaZero: policy only 1777, value only 1992, with 400 MCTS simulations 2470. Leela Chess Zero: policy only 2292, value only 2418, with 400 MCTS 2858.
limits: Engines were trained differently and use different inputs. Authors say direct comparison has caveats.
agent_relevance: Matches the idea of a fast first option plus selective checking: search on top of recognition adds 300-500 Elo here.

source: Ruoss et al. (2024) Amortized planning with large-scale transformers
finding: A concrete unusual-situation failure of pure recognition: the state-only model cannot see move history, so it misses threefold repetition. Authors patch it by checking the move before playing it.
numbers: Patch: if the next move would trigger repetition when the win estimate is above 99%, pick another move.
limits: The patch is hand-made; the model cannot plan around the risk.
agent_relevance: A scaffold needs a short rule check after the first option, because recognition cannot see what is not in the input.

source: Schultz et al. (2025) Mastering board games by external and internal planning with language models
finding: A language model used as policy and value with no search reaches an external Elo near 2900. Search on top gives gains that grow with search budget.
numbers: Searchless MAV external Elo 2923 (mean scoring), 2875 (max scoring). MAV plus MCTS with 100 simulations: internal Elo 68 higher than searchless MAV; Elo grows roughly logarithmically with simulations. Authors report about +300 Elo with a fairly limited budget. 14,689 chess games in the tournament.
limits: Domain-specific fine-tuning on chess, not a general chat model. Elo anchored to Stockfish levels; internal and external scales differ.
agent_relevance: A direct AI analogue of recognise first, simulate to check. Small search buys a lot, with diminishing returns.

source: Schultz et al. (2025) Mastering board games by external and internal planning with language models
finding: Internal search: the model writes a linearised search tree in text and then picks a move. In the paper's worked example it changes its first choice after looking deeper.
numbers: Example: first prediction Qd6; after exploring the top 3 lines one step further it picks Qxg6.
limits: One worked example, not a rate. Training on search traces is required; this does not appear from prompting alone.
agent_relevance: A trained version of first option, then simulate, then maybe switch. A prompted agent has no such step unless the scaffold forces it.

source: Schultz et al. (2025) Mastering board games by external and internal planning with language models
finding: Return on search falls with each doubling, and differs by game.
numbers: Chess Elo rises logarithmically with simulations and with test-time tokens. Other games sit on different Elo scales (for example Connect Four internal Elo 0 to 499 in the table).
limits: Per-game tables not fully read.
agent_relevance: Cap the number of checking passes; the next pass buys less.

source: Zhang et al. (2024) Transcendence: generative models can outperform the experts that train them
finding: A chess transformer trained on human games can beat every player in its data when sampled at low temperature. The most likely first option is a denoised average, not a noisy copy.
numbers: ChessFormer 1000 and 1300 reached about 1500 rating at temperature 0.001. ChessFormer 1500 did not transcend. ChessFormer 1000 about 1450 vs Stockfish level 1 at 1550.
limits: Authors argue it needs data diversity (fails in the 1500 case). Chess only, small models.
agent_relevance: A low-variance first option beats a single expert sample here. Supports a first-option mode with low sampling variance, but it fails when experience is narrow.

source: Karvonen (2024) Emergent world models and latent variable estimation in chess-playing language models
finding: A GPT trained only on game text holds an internal board state and estimates player skill. Adding a skill direction improves play.
numbers: 16-layer model: legal-move rate 99.8%; win rate 64% vs Stockfish level 0 (about 1300 Elo); 8-layer 46%. Linear probe for squares 99.6% accurate (random-weights baseline 74.7%); skill probe 90.5%. The skill vector raised win rate up to 2.6 times.
limits: Small model, weak opponent. Probe accuracy shows information is present, not that it is used the way people use patterns.
agent_relevance: A model trained on experience infers whom it imitates and acts accordingly. Naming an expert level in the prompt may shift the first option.

source: Toshniwal, Wiseman, Livescu, Gimpel (2022) Chess as a testbed for language model state tracking
finding: Language models can track pieces and predict legal moves from move strings alone given enough data. Board-state supervision helps when data is small. Full attention over the game history is needed.
numbers: Three findings in the abstract; numbers not copied.
limits: Abstract and head of the paper only. Trained from scratch, not a prompted chat model.
agent_relevance: Recognising the state is the first step in RPD. Here state tracking is learnable but fragile with less data or truncated history.

source: Kahneman and Klein (2009) Conditions for intuitive expertise: a failure to disagree
finding: The two camps agree: intuition can be trusted when the environment is regular enough and the person had a chance to learn it. Felt confidence is not a good guide to accuracy.
numbers: No numbers in the abstract.
quote: Subjective experience is not a reliable indicator of judgment accuracy.
limits: Abstract only. Argument paper, not new data.
agent_relevance: Gives a mode rule: first-option mode only when the domain is regular and we have relevant experience; confidence alone is not the gate.

source: Wikipedia, Recognition primed decision
finding: The entry lists chess players among RPD users and says the model needs extensive experience and can fail in unusual or misidentified situations. It has a citation-needed tag and no numbers.
numbers: None given.
limits: Weak source: one cited book (Klein 1998), no experiments. It is the origin of this subfield's row.
agent_relevance: The row rests on a weak secondary source. The chess studies above give a mixed picture.

source: Vidulich & Tsang (2026) Intuition and deliberation in elite expertise, discussion
finding: The authors argue RPD-style training on repeated typical scenes is not enough for novel emergencies; training must build knowledge for deliberation and procedures for novel events. They note search plus learned intuition beat either alone in AI.
numbers: No numbers.
quote: Deliberative processes will almost certainly be called upon during unprecedented or rarely practiced scenarios
limits: Position statement. The training proposal is not tested in this paper.
agent_relevance: Matches the fails-in-unusual-situations boundary: add a novelty check that moves to deliberate mode.

source: Klein, Calderwood, Clinton-Cirocco (1986) Rapid decision making on the fire ground (via search-result summary of Klein 2010)
finding: Founding fireground study. A later summary says that in fewer than 12% of critical decision points was there evidence of comparing alternatives.
numbers: Fewer than 12% of critical decision points showed option comparison (figure from a search summary of Klein 2010; I did not verify it in the primary text).
limits: Not opened. Recall interviews, no control group, no outcome measure. Interview coding can read comparison out of the data.
agent_relevance: The fireground base rate is a coded interview figure, not an accuracy result.

source: Johnson and Raab (2003) Take the first: option generation and resulting choices
finding: Handball experts' first-generated option was usually good, and generating more options tended to lower choice quality. Main lab support for first workable option.
numbers: Not opened; no numbers recorded.
limits: Not opened. Sport task; the 2026 Raab replication is in the E04 folder and found task and time moderators.
agent_relevance: Supports first-option mode when the domain is familiar and time is short.
